**ARGUMENT**

**The Adverse Credibility Finding Cannot Stand Unless It Rests on Specific, Cogent Reasons Bearing a Legitimate Nexus to the Finding.**

This Court reviews the agency's credibility determination for substantial evidence, and its findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary. 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B). That deference is considerable, but it presupposes a reasoned finding that the Court can examine. An Immigration Judge ("IJ") who rejects an applicant's testimony must give specific, cogent reasons for doing so, and those reasons must bear a legitimate nexus to the finding. *Secaida-Rosales v. INS*, 331 F.3d 297, 307 (2d Cir. 2003), *superseded by statute on other grounds as recognized in Xiu Xia Lin v. Mukasey*, 534 F.3d 162, 167 (2d Cir. 2008).

The REAL ID Act of 2005 did not eliminate the requirement of a reasoned, record-based explanation. For applications it governs, an IJ may consider demeanor, candor, responsiveness, plausibility, consistency, and other relevant factors, "without regard to whether" an inconsistency, inaccuracy, or falsehood goes to the heart of the claim. 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(1)(B)(iii). The statute thus displaced *Secaida-Rosales*'s heart-of-the-claim rule. But it requires that the determination rest on "the totality of the circumstances, and all relevant factors." *Id.*; *see Xiu Xia Lin*, 534 F.3d at 167 (IJ may rely on any inconsistency or omission so long as the totality of the circumstances establishes that the applicant is not credible). Latitude to consider a collateral discrepancy is not license to treat every discrepancy as decisive. The agency must still connect the cited matter to a conclusion that the applicant is not worthy of belief.

Accordingly, this Court examines whether each stated reason is supported by the record and carries the weight assigned to it. In *Hong Fei Gao v. Sessions*, 891 F.3d 67, 78–79 (2d Cir. 2018), the Court explained that omissions are generally less probative than direct contradictions and that their significance depends on context, including whether the applicant would reasonably have been expected to disclose the omitted information. An IJ who relies on an omission without meaningfully assessing that context has not shown why it undermines credibility.

The same discipline governs implausibility findings and inferences. An IJ may draw reasonable inferences from the evidence, but an inference must be tethered to record facts, viewed in light of common sense and ordinary experience; bare speculation will not do. *See Siewe v. Gonzales*, 480 F.3d 160, 168–69 (2d Cir. 2007). Likewise, before relying on discrepancies between testimony and an earlier interview, the agency must be satisfied that the interview record is reliable. *Ramsameachire v. Ashcroft*, 357 F.3d 169, 179–81 (2d Cir. 2004) (identifying factors bearing on the reliability of airport interview statements). A discrepancy drawn from an unreliable source has little logical bearing on whether the applicant testified truthfully.

Here, the IJ's stated reasons fail these standards. [Identify each reason, with record citations, and show that it (1) misstates the record; (2) rests on speculation; (3) relies on a trivial or illusory discrepancy or omission; (4) disregards a plausible explanation or corroborating evidence; or (5) draws on an unreliable prior statement.]

These defects require vacatur and remand. When an adverse credibility determination rests in part on erroneous reasons, the Court may affirm only if it can confidently predict that the agency would reach the same decision absent the errors. *See Cao He Lin v. U.S. Dep't of Justice*, 428 F.3d 391, 401–02 (2d Cir. 2005). No such confidence is warranted where, as here, the flawed reasons are central to the agency's analysis and the remaining reasons cannot independently sustain it. [Explain why, citing the IJ's and Board's decisions.] Nor may the government salvage the ruling by supplying rationales the agency never adopted. *See SEC v. Chenery Corp.*, 318 U.S. 80, 94–95 (1943). The petition should be granted, the agency's decision vacated, and the case remanded.
